notes.meaning: Jehoshaphat took the throne after his father Asa died and promptly secured the northern border against the rival kingdom of Israel. He prepared Judah's defenses so the people would be safe from sudden attack. Good leaders take wise steps to protect those in their care.

The new king placed troops in all of Judah's walled towns to strengthen their defenses. He also placed military outposts throughout the countryside and in the northern towns his father had earlier captured. By stationing his soldiers carefully, he safeguarded the entire country against enemy invasions.

The Lord stood with Jehoshaphat because the king followed the faithful example set by his ancestor David in his earlier years. Instead of chasing after the false Canaanite gods known as Baals, he prayed to the true God of his ancestors. He kept God's commands rather than copying the idol worship practiced in northern Israel.

Because Jehoshaphat honored God, the Lord made his royal authority strong and secure over the land. The people of Judah respected their king and brought him voluntary gifts, which gave him great wealth and honor. When a leader acts righteously, God often unites the people in loyalty.

Jehoshaphat took great courage and delight in serving the Lord with all his heart. His faith moved him to act boldly by removing pagan worship places and wooden poles set up for the false goddess Asherah. He wanted nothing to distract his people from pure devotion to God.

In his third year as king, Jehoshaphat organized a major plan to instruct the people in God's truth. He appointed five royal officials to lend the king's authority to the mission. They were accompanied by nine Levites and two priests, who were trained ministers of God's house, so they could explain the law to the crowds.

These teachers traveled from town to town throughout Judah, carrying the written scroll of God's law with them. They read and explained the scriptures so that everyday citizens could understand how God wanted them to live. A community grows strong when its members are grounded in the word of God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars view this nationwide teaching tour as an idealized story created by the Chronicler to highlight the importance of the law after the exile, rather than an actual event from Jehoshaphat's reign.

notes.meaning: The Lord caused a deep, holy fear to fall on all the kingdoms bordering Judah, so none of them dared to make war against Jehoshaphat. While the king focused on teaching God's word, God protected the nation from outside trouble. Obeying God brings a peace that human weapons alone cannot provide.

Surrounding nations recognized Jehoshaphat's strength and God's favor upon him, so they paid tribute to keep the peace. Some Philistines brought large gifts of silver, and neighboring Arab tribes brought thousands of rams and goats from their flocks. God gave Judah respect and prosperity in the eyes of their former enemies.

Jehoshaphat continued to grow greater and more powerful with each passing year. He launched major building projects across Judah, constructing strong fortresses and special store cities. These places were used to safely store grain, food supplies, and armor in case of an invasion.

The king kept abundant provisions and materials ready in the cities of Judah to meet any national need. In the capital city of Jerusalem, he also kept a force of seasoned and valiant warriors. His careful planning ensured that both food and defenders were ready for any challenge.

The fighting men of Judah were organized according to their family clans under three main commanders. Adnah led the first and largest group of three hundred thousand valiant soldiers. Beside him, Jehohanan led two hundred and eighty thousand men, while Amasiah, who had gladly offered himself to serve the Lord, led two hundred thousand.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars suggest that the huge troop totals reflect a later misunderstanding of the Hebrew term for thousand, which may originally have meant a much smaller family unit or military squad.

notes.meaning: The soldiers from the neighboring tribe of Benjamin were grouped under two trusted leaders. Eliada commanded two hundred thousand men armed with bows and shields, weapons the tribe of Benjamin was famous for using. Next to him, Jehozabad led another one hundred and eighty thousand men fully equipped and trained for battle.

All these commanders and their men were registered to serve the king at the royal court in Jerusalem. They stood ready to assemble whenever the king called on them for duty. These central forces were in addition to the troops already stationed inside the fortified cities throughout Judah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see the army total of 1,160,000 men as unrealistically large for such a small region, suggesting the numbers were either damaged in copying or exaggerated to emphasize God's blessing.
